content: The immunization system must address routine immunization gaps, implement accelerated disease control and elimination initiatives, and integrate the seven core components of the immunization system. It is essential to consider barriers within the health system and the broader context in which these programs operate. A comprehensive analysis of the immunization system components and health system barriers is necessary. This includes findings from sector reviews, Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) reviews, Effective Vaccine Management (EVM) assessments, data quality assessments, post-introduction evaluations, and coverage surveys. These findings should be integrated into a situation analysis to inform strategies. The national immunization program should establish a set of objectives and milestones for the next five years. These objectives should align with national, regional, and global immunization and public health goals. The objectives must be clearly defined, milestones set, and priorities established through a structured process. Strategies to achieve immunization objectives should address identified weaknesses and build on existing strengths. These strategies must include program management plans, human resource management plans, costing and financing analyses, vaccine and logistics plans, immunization service plans, monitoring and surveillance frameworks, and demand generation and communication plans. These strategies should also align with national and global health goals to ensure synergy and comprehensiveness. An activity timeline and a monitoring and evaluation framework should be developed to track progress toward immunization targets. This framework must include systematic data collection, sub-national indicator tracking, supervision programs, and research. A detailed monitoring and evaluation plan should be documented, including data analysis and surveillance reviews. The financial section of the plan should outline overall costs, funding sources, and financial gaps. A resource mobilization strategy must be developed to address these gaps and ensure sustainability. This includes identifying sources of finance, creating a sustainability plan, and ensuring the immunization program is fully funded. The implementation of the comprehensive multi-year plan (cMYP) should be supported by annual operational plans (AOPs) at both national and sub-national levels. These plans should include budget requests, planning, monitoring, and surveillance reviews. Political endorsement from relevant ministries is critical to ensure the plan's success. The cMYP should also include a situation analysis of accelerated disease control initiatives, such as polio, measles, rubella, and neonatal tetanus. Indicators like vaccination coverage, disease surveillance, and campaign effectiveness should be monitored. Similarly, routine EPI performance should be assessed by analyzing immunization coverage, equity, demand, and the introduction of new vaccines. Program management must ensure that legal and regulatory frameworks are in place to support immunization financing and policy updates. Annual work plans and micro-plans for immunization should be developed and funded through national budgeting processes. Coordination mechanisms, such as Interagency Coordination Committees (ICCs) and National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs), should be strengthened. Human resource management should focus on training health workers in immunization services, addressing workforce gaps, and conducting regular supervision. Pre-service medical and nursing curricula should include immunization education. Costing and financing strategies must ensure financial sustainability by increasing government funding for routine vaccines and monitoring expenditures at all levels. Sub-national immunization budgets should be tracked and reported nationally. Vaccine supply and logistics must ensure adequate cold-chain equipment, waste management policies, and reliable vaccine delivery systems. Regular inventory assessments and maintenance of cold-chain equipment are essential. Surveillance and reporting systems should monitor routine immunization coverage, adverse events following immunization (AEFI), and disease outbreaks. Sentinel surveillance for diseases like rotavirus and meningitis should be established. National immunization objectives and milestones should focus on improving immunization coverage, addressing inequities, and introducing new vaccines. Strategies should include engaging underserved communities, leveraging technology, and integrating immunization into broader health and education systems. Advocacy efforts should involve civil society organizations (CSOs), professional associations, and opinion leaders to promote the value of immunization. Communication strategies should address vaccine hesitancy and misinformation while leveraging social media and other technologies. Efforts to address inequities should include tailored strategies for marginalized groups, urban areas, and conflict zones. A life-course approach to immunization planning should be adopted to ensure equitable access across all age groups. Finally, community engagement should involve tracking individual immunization statuses, utilizing community structures, and training health workers and CSOs to engage effectively with communities. New approaches to urban and peri-urban outreach should be developed to meet the needs of diverse populations.
